items.summary:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server fetched caller-supplied pipeline package URLs without restricting the destination. A caller authorized to create a pipeline or pipeline version could cause requests to originate from the API server's network position, including to internal services that the caller could not otherwise reach.

## Impact

The reported evidence demonstrates blind server-side request forgery and a limited status-code oracle. The fetched response is processed as a pipeline package; the report does not demonstrate arbitrary response-body disclosure or credential theft. A request to a cloud metadata endpoint returned HTTP 403, which does not establish access to metadata contents or tokens.

The confidentiality metric is Low to reflect the limited information obtainable through the status-code oracle. High confidentiality impact and integrity or availability impact are not established by the submitted evidence. Impact depends on the API server's network reachability and the deployment's trust boundaries.

## Patches

Fixed by [kubeflow/pipelines#12750](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12750), first released in 2.17.0. The fix validates URL schemes, ports, allowed domains, and resolved IP addresses; validates redirects; and enforces IP restrictions at connection time. The HTTP client also applies timeouts and disables environment proxy use so connections pass through the validated dialer.

Operators should keep pipeline URL validation enabled and limit additional allowed domains to trusted pipeline sources.

## Workarounds

Until upgrading, restrict API-server egress to required destinations through deployment-specific network controls. Account for required Kubernetes and storage connectivity when applying these restrictions.

## Related reports

This is the canonical advisory for the API-server pipeline URL SSRF family. [GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv) is tracked as a duplicate submission. Each submission retains its own reporter attribution; this cross-link does not transfer authorship.

## Earlier related submission

@pwny0's [GHSA-fxx8-rx8w-p9v7](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-fxx8-rx8w-p9v7), submitted September 23, 2023, included an earlier report of external interaction through the API-server pipeline-package URL path. That portion is consolidated here; its namespace-based frontend SSRF is tracked separately under [GHSA-895m-3hxm-h4mg](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-895m-3hxm-h4mg) / CVE-2023-6570.

This acknowledges the earlier pipeline-URL submission without attributing fxx8's frontend response-disclosure or cookie-forwarding evidence to the API-server path. @pwny0 retains reporter credit on fxx8; @gasbugs retains reporter credit for this submission. Neither report's authorship is transferred.

items.summary:
### Summary
Remark42 applied chi's `middleware.RealIP` globally, trusting `True-Client-IP` / `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-For` headers without verifying the request came from a trusted proxy. The per-IP rate limiters key on the overwritten `r.RemoteAddr`, so any client can bypass every per-IP rate limiter by rotating spoofed IP headers. The same spoofed IP also drives other per-IP controls (stored comment IP, anonymous identity derivation, and `--votes-ip` vote de-duplication). This affects deployments reachable directly from the internet (Remark42's built-in HTTP, static TLS, and ACME modes are all documented and supported), as well as any proxied deployment where the proxy forwards an attacker-controlled recognised header.

### Details
The router applies `middleware.RealIP` globally, ahead of the per-route limiters, without any check that the server is behind a trusted proxy (in v1.16.1, `backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:207`).

The `rateLimiter` function (v1.16.1, `backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:769-779`) builds a tollbooth limiter with `IPLookup{Name: "RemoteAddr"}`, which reads `r.RemoteAddr`. Since chi's `middleware.RealIP` (v1.16.1, `backend/vendor/github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware/realip.go:42-55`) unconditionally overwrites `r.RemoteAddr` from `True-Client-IP > X-Real-IP > first X-Forwarded-For` (accepting any syntactically valid IP), any client can set its apparent IP to an arbitrary value.

This bypasses every per-IP rate limiter that runs after `RealIP`: `/auth` (2/s), avatars (100/s), the image proxy (10/s), open / protected / admin route groups (10/s), root routes (50/s), and `/web/*` (20/s). Comment and vote creation go through the update limiter, whose server default is `UPDATE_LIMIT=0.5`/s (burst 1), not 10/s. The global 1,000 concurrent-request throttle still applies, so this is a per-IP-limit bypass rather than truly unlimited throughput. chi's own documentation warns that `middleware.RealIP` should be used only behind a trusted proxy.

### PoC
```bash
# Deploy Remark42 reachable directly from the internet (built-in HTTP / TLS / ACME, no proxy that overwrites the headers).
# Comment creation is limited to UPDATE_LIMIT (default 0.5/s, burst 1) per IP.

# Rotate X-Real-IP across many requests; each distinct value gets its own token bucket.
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
    -H "X-Real-IP: 192.0.2.$i" \
    -X POST 'https://remark42.example.com/api/v1/comment?site=site1' \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"text":"spam","locator":{"site":"site1","url":"https://example.com/post"}}'
done | sort | uniq -c
# With rotating headers the responses stay 201; without them, requests beyond the burst return 429.
```

### Impact
By rotating the spoofed client IP an attacker bypasses the per-IP token buckets on all rate-limited endpoints and defeats other per-IP controls, enabling: (a) spam comment creation beyond the configured per-IP limit, (b) confirmation-email / notification flooding to supplied addresses, (c) high-volume outbound image fetching and resource consumption via the image proxy (its transport still blocks private/reserved destinations and DNS rebinding, so this is amplification, not new SSRF reach), (d) authentication-endpoint abuse, (e) where `--votes-ip` is enabled, defeating per-IP vote de-duplication (ballot stuffing), and (f) minting fresh anonymous identities and poisoning the stored comment IP and request logs, since the anonymous user ID is derived from `name + RemoteAddr`. The global concurrency ceiling and per-request timeouts remain, so availability impact is limited.

### Resolution
Mitigation support was added in v1.16.2 (umputun/remark42#2116, follow-up in #2118). **Upgrading alone does not remediate the issue: `--trusted-proxy` must be configured.**

The fix adds `--trusted-proxy` / `TRUSTED_PROXY`. When set, the forwarding headers (`X-Real-IP`, then `CF-Connecting-IP`, then the leftmost public `X-Forw

items.summary:
### Summary
A remote attacker from any IP address defeats the operator-configured source-IP allowlist (`mcp_allowed_remote_ips` / `api_token_allowed_remote_ips`) by sending a single `X-Forwarded-For: <allowlisted-ip>` header. The router is created with `gin.New()` and never calls `SetTrustedProxies`, so gin trusts every proxy by default and `c.ClientIP()` returns the attacker-supplied header verbatim. The same forged value is also written to `Transaction.CreatedIp` and the access log, so the attacker's real IP never appears in any record.

### Details
`cmd/webserver.go:104` builds the router with `gin.New()`. A grep of `cmd/` and `pkg/` confirms `SetTrustedProxies` is never called, leaving gin's default trusted-proxy range of `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0`. `WebContext` (`pkg/core/context_web.go:39`) embeds `*gin.Context` and does not override `ClientIP()`.

Both allowlist middlewares match the operator allowlist against this attacker-controlled value:

```go
// pkg/middlewares/mcp_server_ip_limit.go:19
if config.MCPAllowedRemoteIPs[i].Match(c.ClientIP()) { c.Next(); return }
```

The identical `c.ClientIP()` is consumed by the audit trail at `pkg/api/transactions.go:1078` (`createNewTransactionModel(..., c.ClientIP())` → `CreatedIp`) and the access log (`pkg/middlewares/request_log.go:28`), so one header both bypasses the gate and forges attribution.

### PoC
Runtime PoC (no live deployment required) — `pkg/middlewares/xff_bypass_runtime_test.go`, `pkg/middlewares/xff_chain_runtime_test.go`:

```
go test ./pkg/middlewares/ -run 'TestACCESSCONTROL001_XFFBypass|TestCHAIN_AllowlistBypass' -v
```

Output:
```
[control] no XFF, RemoteAddr=1.2.3.4 -> status=400 (correctly blocked)
[exploit] XFF=10.0.0.1, RemoteAddr=1.2.3.4 -> status=200, ClientIP=10.0.0.1 (bypassed)
gate status = 200 | created_ip that would be persisted = "10.0.0.1"
```

Against a live instance with `mcp_allowed_remote_ips=10.0.0.1`:
```
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://target/mcp            # 403 (blocked)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1" https://target/mcp  # passes IP gate
```

### Impact
Defeats an explicitly advertised, operator-configured security control on the MCP and API-token surfaces, from any source IP, with a single header and no authentication to the gate itself. It also destroys non-repudiation: every action is logged under the spoofed allowlisted IP, so audit trails point at the trusted host instead of the attacker. (The MCP/API actions themselves still require a valid token — this neutralizes the compensating IP control, not the JWT layer.)

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) present significant challenges to source tracing of generated code, as LLM rewriting can substantially alter the syntactic and structural characteristics of watermarked code. However, existing watermarking methods often suffer severe performance degradation under LLM-based functionality-preserving rewriting attacks. We attribute this vulnerability not merely to the intensity of rewriting, but to a fundamental distribution mismatch between the perturbations encountered during watermark training and the global, non-deterministic rewriting behaviors induced by LLMs. In order to deal with this challenge, we propose RoCoMark, a Robust Code waterMarking framework that explicitly learns and adapts to LLM rewriting behaviors. RoCoMark is a multi-round minimax game between the watermark embedder and LLM rewriter. In each round, the embedder first learns threat profiling from LLM-rewritten code by optimizing the watermark encoder through contrastive learning and knowledge distillation while mitigating catastrophic representation drift. Then the embedder improves strategies by optimizing the watermark encoder and extractor simultaneously. Finally, an adaptive attack-evolution mechanism based on Reflexion and short- and long-term memory pools is applied, enabling continuous interaction between the watermark embedder and evolving rewriting strategies. This iterative attacker-defender process progressively improves the robustness of the watermark against diverse and previously unseen LLM rewriting behaviors. Extensive experiments on four typical benchmarks, under attacks generated by five LLMs, show the effectiveness of RoCoMark. RoCoMark achieves an average detection AUROC of 74.2% and a Rewrite BitACC of 75.3%, while maintaining a code functionality pass rate above 99.7%.
items.title: RoCoMark: Robust Code Watermarking Against LLM-Based Functionality-Preserving Rewriting Attacks

items.summary: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects. In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions. Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.
items.title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems

items.summary: Modern software systems routinely process credentials, personal records, and other sensitive information. A sensitive information exposure (SIEx) defect makes such information accessible to an unauthorized actor and can cause serious and often irreversible disclosure. However, prior research has focused largely on detecting such exposures rather than repairing the underlying defects, and existing repository-level issue-resolution benchmarks do not specifically target this defect class. We present SIExBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark dedicated to automated repair of SIEx defects. SIExBench contains 161 execution-verified instances from 64 widely used Python and Java repositories, each with an issue report, buggy repository snapshot, developer patch, executable exposure and regression tests, and defect characterization. We evaluate six repair systems with three LLMs, yielding 18 configurations, and systematically analyze their overall effectiveness, performance across defect characteristics, and failure mechanisms. The strongest configuration resolves only 39.1% of the instances, while 40.4% remain unresolved by all 18 configurations. More importantly, 62.1% of unsuccessful attempts produce a valid patch that still leaves sensitive information exposed, making incomplete exposure removal a central challenge. Systems often generate plausible patches and modify relevant code without fully eliminating the exposure, indicating that effective repair must ensure that all relevant paths to sensitive-information exposure are closed. Overall, SIExBench provides a foundation for systematically evaluating and advancing automated repair of sensitive information exposure defects.
items.title: SIExBench: A Benchmark for Automated Repair of Sensitive Information Exposure

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as shared multi-tenant services, relying on advanced optimizations like KV cache and prefix sharing to improve throughput and reduce latency. However, these optimizations introduce a critical vulnerability: attackers can exploit time-to-first-token (TTFT) variations between KV cache hits and misses to infer sensitive prompt tokens via prefix-matching side-channel attacks. Existing defenses indiscriminately restrict cross-tenant cache sharing, which incurs prohibitive performance overhead and negates the fundamental efficiency benefits of the KV cache. We propose Mirage, a topology-aware emission obfuscation framework that provably bounds timing leakage without sacrificing the performance gains of cache sharing. Instead of stalling the GPU or forcing redundant recomputations, Mirage delays token emission at the gateway so the attacker observes a natural cache miss distribution, while the GPU seamlessly continues serving other requests at full speed. Mirage uses a Privacy Odometer that persistently tracks the topological novelty of prefix fan-out expansions to distinguish aggressive probing from benign traffic. Once a prefix exceeds a safety threshold, Mirage engages a two-phase policy that uses a dynamic estimator to pad the TTFT to a calibrated cache-miss baseline. On a 500-sample public corpus across three models, Mirage suppresses the timing side-channel to near the random-guessing floor, while maintaining a significantly lower TTFT than defense baselines. We further show that Mirage withstands a strong adaptive adversary and the same principle carries over to semantic caching layers.
items.title: Mirage: Provable Defense Against LLM KV Cache Timing Side Channels with Topology-Aware Isolation

items.summary: Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand. We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave. They build on three tools that we contribute: (a) ffibox, Rust primitives for C/Rust interop that mirror Box, Arc, and Vec for C objects without ever forming a reference to memory that C may alias; (b) Wavefront, a neuro-symbolic static analyzer that orders a target's items by their dependencies, including those that casts and type-erased pointers hide; and (c) ffimap, a rustc-based analysis that maps the unsafe surface of bindings. On libgit2 and ffmpeg, with one developer in the loop, Crustify generated safe bindings for 41.9% and 42.8% of their public APIs in about 51.9 and 58.9 hours. On the interface consumers are expected to use, only 1.6% and 0.4% of the bindings' public functions are unsafe, and only 0.1% and 0.6% have a raw pointer in their signature. Their tests cover 98.92% and 99.07% of the Rust code and 45.95% and 67.20% of libgit2 and of ffmpeg's libavutil, and the reviewers fixed 8 and 13 defects that caused UB reachable from Rust. To our knowledge, this is the first work to automate the generation of safe Rust bindings for C libraries.
items.title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing

items.summary: Despite undergoing safety training to align with human values, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that circumvent built-in safeguards and elicit malicious behaviors given by the adversary. Existing defenses are mostly static and fail to adapt to new or unknown attack strategies, providing limited resilience. To address these, we propose a multi-agent defense framework, GuardrailAgent, that offers adaptive, end-to-end protection. The system autonomously gathers and summarizes attack characteristics into a continuously updated knowledge base that supports both input- and output-side detection. A feedback module integrates misclassified cases for iterative improvement at minimal cost. Tested on over ten representative jailbreaks, the framework achieved a 93.1% input-side detection rate, 93.9% overall detection, and a 95.8% F1 score, while rapidly adapting to unseen attacks. These results demonstrate GuardrailAgent's outstanding capability to maintain LLM safety in the face of evolving jailbreak tactics.
items.title: GuardrailAgent: An Agentic Framework for Jailbreak Defense

items.summary: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.

From 0.6.0.beta1 until 0.7.1, there is insufficient isolation between execution-capable Docker sandboxes and trusted application services. A low-privileged authenticated user who can execute commands in their own sandbox can reach other tenants' sandbox APIs, access their files and secrets, execute commands in active sandboxes, and enumerate, create, or delete sandboxes through the unauthenticated provisioner without knowing administrator, database, or MinIO credentials. Sandboxes can also reach shared internal services; if shipped default service credentials remain unchanged, an attacker can use them, and if the exposed PostgreSQL account is a superuser, obtain command execution in the PostgreSQL container. These paths can disclose or modify cross-tenant data and sandbox state or cause denial of service through sandbox deletion without a container escape or kernel vulnerability. This vulnerability is fixed in 0.7.1. Existing deployments must separately rotate persisted PostgreSQL, Neo4j, or MinIO credentials that were previously set to documented or shipped defaults because upgrading the Compose files does not automatically rotate them.

items.summary:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines frontend reflected untrusted pod names and namespaces into HTML error responses from the pod-information and pod-events routes. An attacker could craft a link that causes JavaScript to execute in the frontend's origin when a user follows it and reaches an affected error response.

Affected routes include `/pipeline/k8s/pod` and `/pipeline/k8s/pod/events` (the deployment's configured base path may differ).

## Impact and prerequisites

Successful exploitation requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied link and reach the vulnerable response. JavaScript execution may expose information accessible to the victim's browser or perform actions in the application's origin.

The attacker does not need an account merely to construct and deliver the link. The victim must satisfy the deployment's authentication and route-access requirements. Cookie theft depends on cookie attributes and deployment protections; it is not guaranteed. The submitted evidence does not establish an availability impact or server-side code execution.

## Technical details

The pod handlers pass `podname` and `podnamespace` query values to `getPod` and `listPodEvents` in `frontend/server/k8s-helper.ts`. Before remediation, failure messages incorporated those values, along with backend error details, and were returned as HTML-capable string responses.

Kubernetes rejecting an invalid resource name did not prevent the issue: the rejected name could still be included in the frontend's error response.

[PR #12295](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12295) changed the error construction to validate pod names and namespaces with `isAllowedResourceName`. Invalid values produce a constant error message instead of reflecting the supplied value, and backend error details are no longer included in these responses. The change includes invalid-resource-name tests.

## Affected versions and remediation

Affected product: the Kubeflow Pipelines frontend server, identified as `ghcr.io/kubeflow/kfp-frontend`. Historical releases may use earlier image registry names.

Upgrade to **KFP 2.15.0 or later**.

The fix merged on October 10, 2025, in commit [fedc25e3f7251933d4a37b964bc3e8176beea28e](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/commit/fedc25e3f7251933d4a37b964bc3e8176beea28e). It is first present in the **2.15.0** release, published November 25, 2025.

The affected range is recorded as `< 2.15.0`. The original introduction version and separate maintenance-branch backports have not been established. These are KFP component versions, not Kubeflow platform or Python SDK versions.

## Distinction from existing artifact XSS

[CVE-2023-6571](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7rvc-xw75-43jf), tracked in the repository as [GHSA-j9xw-rrjg-2p9r](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-j9xw-rrjg-2p9r), documents reflection of the artifact `source` parameter in an unknown-storage-source error.

This report concerns different handlers and error construction: pod information and pod events. The artifact-source fix in [PR #9844](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/9844), released in 2.0.2, did not repair these pod responses. They required the later change in #12295.

This independently fixable pod-route defect is tracked as CVE-2026-88986. It does not broaden CVE-2023-6571 or absorb artifact-content rendering and other XSS reports.

## Attribution

**@pwny0** submitted this report on September 23, 2023, and retains the reporter credit.

**@JerT33** authored the remediation in PR #12295. Fix attribution is separate from vulnerability-report attribution.

items.summary:
## Summary

The `sql()` VQL plugin runs a caller-supplied database driver and connection string with no permission check (`vql/parsers/sql/sql.go:93`, `SQLPlugin.Call`). For `driver='mysql'` or `driver='postgres'` the handle comes from `GetHandleOther` (`sql.go:39`), which passes the connection string straight to Go `database/sql` `sql.Open` (`sql.go:51`) and executes the query (`sql.go:159`).

The plugin declares `FILESYSTEM_READ` only as `Info().Permissions` metadata (`sql.go:219`). That metadata is never consulted at runtime: `metadata.go:19` stores it as a string that only the documentation exporter reads (`api/reflect.go:82-110`). Every sibling network plugin (`http_client`, `netcat`, `s3`, `rsyslog`) calls `CheckAccess(acls.NETWORK)` in its own body; `sql()` calls nothing.

The built-in `analyst` role holds `ANY_QUERY` but not `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK` (`acls/roles.go:222`), and reaches this sink through the notebook query API.

Result: a low-priv analyst opens arbitrary outbound TCP connections and, through a rogue MySQL server's `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE`, reads any file the root-running server can read, including the deployment CA private key.

## Affected

- Velocidex/velociraptor server, `<= v0.77.1` (latest release, 2026-06-23). Identical vulnerable code in `master` HEAD `1961e79` (2026-07-17).
- Confirmed live-exploitable on the official `ghcr.io/velocidex/velociraptor-server:latest` image (build 0.77.1, commit bbe2a58).
- Stock install, default Basic authenticator, any built-in `analyst`, `investigator`, or `api` role (all hold `ANY_QUERY`, none holds `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK`).
- No non-default flag required.

## Root cause

`SQLPlugin.Call` (`vql/parsers/sql/sql.go:93`) parses the caller `driver`, `connstring`, and `query` arguments and reaches `handle.Query` (`sql.go:159`) without any `vql_subsystem.CheckAccess` call in its body. For `driver='mysql'` or `driver='postgres'` the handle comes from `GetHandleOther` (`sql.go:39`), which hands the attacker connection string to `sql.Open` (`sql.go:51`), so the plugin dials an arbitrary host and, through the MySQL client `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` feature, reads local files. The plugin states its intended gate only as metadata, `VQLMetadata().Permissions(acls.FILESYSTEM_READ)` (`sql.go:219`), but `MetadataBuilder.Permissions` merely stores a string (`vql/metadata.go:19`) that is read only by the reflection exporter (`api/reflect.go:82-110`), never by the query engine. Every sibling network plugin enforces `CheckAccess(acls.NETWORK)` in its own body, so the omission in `sql()` is an enforcement oversight. The default `analyst` role grants `ANY_QUERY` without `FILESYSTEM_READ` or `NETWORK` (`acls/roles.go:222`), so a user the operator deliberately restricted still reaches the ungated sink.

Note on intent: `acls/acls.go` documents that specific permission combinations grant admin-equivalent power (`SERVER_ARTIFACT_WRITER` with `COLLECT_SERVER`, `ARTIFACT_WRITER` with `COLLECT_CLIENT`), but the `analyst` role holds none of them and is denied `EXECVE`, `NETWORK`, and `FILESYSTEM_READ` on every sibling plugin. If `ANY_QUERY` is nonetheless intended as trusted, the plugin's own `Permissions(FILESYSTEM_READ)` metadata and the runtime enforcement on all sibling plugins are misleading and should be reconciled; otherwise this is a missing runtime check.

## Reproduction

`ghcr.io/velocidex/velociraptor-server:latest` (v0.77.1), default config, GUI on `https://localhost:8889`, one built-in `analyst` user.

1) As `analyst`, confirm the control: the gated accessor denies the read.

    sql(driver='sqlite', accessor='file', file='/etc/passwd', query='SELECT 1')
    => sql: Field file Accessor file: PermissionDenied: Permission denied: [FILESYSTEM_READ]

2) Start a rogue MySQL server on an attacker host that completes the handshake and answers any query with a `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE <target>` packet.

3) As the same `analyst`, call the ungated branch through the notebook quer

items.summary: Code Graph RAG is an AI-powered knowledge graph and retrieval system for querying, understanding, and editing multi-language codebases. Prior to 0.0.345, the MCPToolsRegistry.read_file implementation in codebase_rag/mcp/tools.py joins attacker-controlled file_path input to project_root without resolving and verifying containment when offset or limit selects the paginated branch. An absolute path causes pathlib to discard the configured root, while relative traversal can also resolve outside it. The protected non-paginated branch uses validate_project_path, but the paginated branch bypasses that validation before opening the path. An unauthenticated caller of a network-exposed HTTP MCP server can therefore read arbitrary UTF-8-readable files available to the server process, including credentials, environment data, private keys, source, and configuration; local callers through the stdio transport can reach the same vulnerable code path. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.345.

items.summary:
Claude Code validated Edit tool targets using point-in-time pathname and symlink resolution that was not bound to the underlying directory inodes or file descriptors. On macOS, a process running inside Claude Code's Bash sandbox could exploit the resulting time-of-check to time-of-use window by atomically swapping an in-workspace parent directory with a symlink after validation completed, causing the unsandboxed Edit implementation to overwrite an attacker-selected user-writable file outside the workspace. Exploiting this required the ability to run attacker-controlled code inside the sandbox, such as through a malicious repository or dependency script.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix automatically. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Claude Code thanks hackerone.com/mahoraga007 (Sunder Singh) for reporting this issue.

items.summary:
## Summary

The CVE-2026-32885 ZipSlip fix added a symlink-target escape check to Untar, but the check rebases an ABSOLUTE symlink target into dest before validating (filepath.Join(dest, "/etc") stays lexically inside dest and passes), while the symlink is then created with the RAW absolute target via os.Symlink(file.Linkname, ...), so a malicious archive plants a host-absolute symlink and a following regular-file entry writes through it, restoring arbitrary host file create/overwrite (reaching $HOME rc-files, hence RCE). Confirmed at HEAD.

## The defect (the symlink check is a no-op for absolute targets)

CVE-2026-32885 (fixed v1.25.2, commit 05cbe299) added a lexical containment check on the entry path and a NEW symlink-target validation. pkg/archive/archive.go, Untar, tar.TypeSymlink case:

```go
if filepath.IsAbs(file.Linkname) {
    resolvedTarget = filepath.Join(dest, file.Linkname)   // line 298: absolute target REBASED into dest
} else {
    resolvedTarget = filepath.Join(fullPathDir, file.Linkname)
}
if !strings.HasPrefix(filepath.Clean(resolvedTarget)+sep, filepath.Clean(dest)+sep) {  // line 302
    return ...escapes destination...                       // line 303
}
_ = os.Remove(fullPath)                                     // line 307
err = os.Symlink(file.Linkname, fullPath)                  // line 310: writes the RAW Linkname
```

For an absolute Linkname like /Users/victim, line 298 computes filepath.Join(dest, "/Users/victim") = dest/Users/victim (lexically inside dest), so the escape check at line 302 PASSES. But line 310 creates the symlink with the raw file.Linkname, so the on-disk symlink dest/link points at the real host path /Users/victim. The value validated (rebased) is not the value written (raw): a check-one-thing / do-another divergence.

Write-through: the archive carries a second regular-file entry whose Name traverses the planted link (e.g. link/.zshrc). Its fullPath is lexically inside dest so the line-238 check passes (that check is purely lexical and does not resolve the symlink), then os.Create follows the planted symlink and overwrites /Users/victim/.zshrc on the host. Overwriting a shell rc-file, git hook, or cron entry yields code execution. Reachable via ddev add-on get <repo|url> (the exact remote-add-on vector the advisory names), and via ddev import-db / import-files. GitHub codeload tarballs preserve symlinks.

## Verification

EXECUTED (go test driving the real Untar): a file was written OUTSIDE dest and Untar returned nil (VULNERABLE); a pre-existing host file was truncated and overwritten with the attacker payload; the negative controls (a relative ../ symlink escape, and a plain ../ file entry) are both correctly rejected, isolating the bug to the absolute-symlink branch. NOT verified: the end-to-end add-on get over the network (the caller chain is source-confirmed); Windows (reliable on macOS/Linux, DDEV's primary hosts). Unzip is NOT affected (tar-only).

## Suggested fix

Reject absolute symlink targets outright (a dev-environment archive has no need to plant host-absolute symlinks), or validate the RAW target that will actually be written rather than a rebased copy. Additionally, resolve symlinks when validating each regular-file entry's parent so a write cannot traverse a previously-planted link (or extract to a staging dir and reject any entry whose realpath escapes). The lexical line-238 check does not defend against a planted symlink.

## Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The write-through is executed-verified with negative controls (an absolute-symlink entry plus a follow-up file entry wrote and overwrote files OUTSIDE dest while relative-escape and plain-ZipSlip controls were correctly rejected), and I confirmed at HEAD that Untar rebases an absolute symlink target into dest for the escape check (line 298) but creates the symlink with the raw absolute target (line 310).

items.summary:
### Summary

The TCP transporter's packet parser (`src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`) reads the packet length field with `Buffer.prototype.readInt32BE`, a signed read. A crafted packet whose length field has the sign bit set yields a negative `length`. The parser then advances past the parsed message with `packet = packet.slice(length)`, but `Buffer.prototype.slice` clamps an out-of-range negative start index to `0`, so the buffer is returned unchanged. The `while (packet.length > 0)` loop condition therefore never becomes false, producing an infinite synchronous loop that blocks the Node.js event loop indefinitely.

### Impact

Any Moleculer node using the TCP transporter can be rendered completely unresponsive by an unauthenticated remote peer sending a single ~10-byte crafted TCP packet, before any protocol handshake or authentication takes place. `TcpReader.onTcpClientConnected` pipes each accepted socket's bytes straight into a fresh `Parser` instance (`socket.pipe(parser)`) with no handshake, so the code path is reachable by any peer able to reach the transporter's listening port. Because Node.js is single-threaded, the hang blocks the entire event loop of the process, taking down every service hosted in it until it is forcibly restarted. TCP transporter endpoints are frequently auto-discovered via UDP broadcast, so any host on the same network segment can reach the port.

Neither the CRC check nor `maxPacketSize` mitigate the issue: the CRC bytes are fully attacker-computable, and `maxPacketSize` bounds the received buffer size, not the value of the length field.

### Affected component

`Parser._write` in `src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`.

### Patch

The fix validates that the decoded length is at least the 6-byte header size before processing, rejecting negative and undersized values (which would otherwise fail to shrink the buffer) with an error on the write callback instead of looping.

### Credit

Reported by xor4xor via the Tidelift security program.

items.summary:
A remote/local attacker who can get a symbolic link included in a source-code repository that code-graph-rag analyzes can cause the `structural_search` and `structural_replace` tools (backed by `AstGrepService`, exposed both as MCP tools and as agentic AI tools) to read and -- via `structural_replace` with `dry_run=False` -- overwrite arbitrary files outside the configured project root, because the tool's path-containment check (`should_skip_path`/`_classify_file`) is performed lexically on the unresolved path and never checks `Path.is_symlink()` or calls `.resolve()`, unlike the project's own (correct) `validate_project_path` decorator used elsewhere.

Tested at commit `90a3ed3cbdc7d3bb8036985b851cc7c9a3ba9c57` (pyproject version 0.0.550), current `main` at test time. Confirmed this commit already contains the fix for the prior advisory (GHSA-vvr2-h2jp-838m: paginated `read_file` path traversal) and the newer HTTP-MCP bearer-auth gate (`_validate_http_exposure` in `codebase_rag/mcp/server.py`) -- this is a distinct, still-open issue on top of those fixes, in a different component with a different root cause and a strictly worse impact (write, not just read).

## Details

`AstGrepService` (`codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py`) backs both the `structural_search` and `structural_replace` MCP/agentic tools. It enumerates candidate files with `os.walk()` and gates each path only through `should_skip_path()`:

- `codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:84-109` (`_iter_source_files`) -- walks `self.project_root` with `os.walk()`; every non-directory dirent returned (including a symlink pointing anywhere on disk) is treated as an in-scope file.
- `codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:61-82` (`_classify_file`) -- the only containment check is `should_skip_path(...)` followed by `abs_path.relative_to(self.project_root)` (line 82); `abs_path` is never resolved, so this check is purely lexical/string-based.
- `codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:80-109` (`should_skip_path`) and `codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:35-37` (`cached_relative_path`) -- computes `rel_path = file_path.relative_to(repo_path)` without ever calling `.resolve()` or `Path.is_symlink()`.
- Read sink: `codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:143-144` (`search`) -- `source = self._read(abs_path)` calls `path.read_text()`, which Python follows through the symlink to its real target.
- Write sink: `codebase_rag/tools/ast_grep_service.py:187-208` (`replace`), line 208 -- `abs_path.write_text(new_source, ...)` when `dry_run=False`, again following the symlink and overwriting the real target file's content.

This is inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase handles the exact same class of risk. The file read/write/edit tools (`file_reader.py`, `file_writer.py`, `file_editor.py`) are all protected by `validate_project_path` (`codebase_rag/decorators.py:73-75`):

```python
full_path = (self.project_root / file_path_str).resolve()
project_root = self.project_root.resolve()
full_path.relative_to(project_root)
```

`.resolve()` follows symlinks before the containment check runs, so those tools correctly reject an out-of-root target. `path_utils.py`'s own `absolute_path_within_project_root()` (`codebase_rag/utils/path_utils.py:156-176`) documents the same principle explicitly in its docstring: "The resolve() calls are load-bearing: containment is checked lexically, so an unresolved .. segment or symlink would escape the root." -- but `should_skip_path()`/`AstGrepService` never applies that pattern.

items.summary:
### Summary

The documented `web.NewHandler` static file server can read files outside `Config.AppDir` when the request path contains URL-encoded dot-segments such as `%2e%2e`. Go's `ServeMux` redirects plain `/../` paths, but it passes encoded dot-segments to the handler after decoding `r.URL.Path`. The handler then calls `filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, r.URL.Path)` without checking that the result remains under `AppDir`, allowing unauthenticated arbitrary file reads with the server process privileges.

### Details

`web/README.md:34-40` documents a network-facing setup:

```go
http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{
  AppDir: "/path/to/webapp",
  Fallback: "/index.html",
  Dev: false,
}))
log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
```

In `web/handler.go:62-75`, the handler takes `r.URL.Path` and joins it directly with `s.config.AppDir`:

```go
pathname := r.URL.Path
filename := filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, pathname)
fi, err := os.Lstat(filename)
```

Later the same resolved filename is opened and copied to the response in `web/handler.go:150-166` for non-HTML/static files. There is no `filepath.IsLocal`, cleaned-relative-path, absolute-root prefix, or symlink-aware containment check before opening the file.

A plain `/../secret.txt` path is redirected by Go's `ServeMux`, but an encoded path such as `/%2e%2e/secret.txt` is decoded into `r.URL.Path == "/../secret.txt"` and reaches the handler. On Linux, `filepath.Join("/tmp/root/app", "/../secret.txt")` resolves to `/tmp/root/secret.txt`, outside the configured app directory.

Source-to-sink chain:

```text
Unauthenticated HTTP request path containing URL-encoded dot-segments
-> net/http decodes path into r.URL.Path
-> documented ServeMux setup passes encoded dot-segment path to web.NewHandler
-> web/handler.go joins Config.AppDir with r.URL.Path
-> os.Lstat/os.Open operate on the escaped path
-> io.Copy returns file contents to the attacker
```

False-positive checks performed:
- Plain dot-segment paths are redirected by `http.ServeMux`, but encoded dot-segments are not blocked and reach the handler.
- The PoC uses the documented `http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(...))` setup, not a custom bypass of ServeMux.
- A control request for `/secret.txt` does not read the outside file; the disclosure requires encoded traversal segments.
- The issue is independent of `Dev`/HMR; it reproduces with `Dev: false`.
- The root cause appears in other handler paths that join app paths, but the static file read path is sufficient to prove arbitrary file disclosure.

Candidate score: 18/18 under the local audit scoring rubric. The handler is documented for network-facing use, the attacker directly controls the request path, the path reaches `os.Open`, file disclosure was reproduced locally, and no root containment mitigation is present.

### PoC

This safe local proof creates an application directory and a sibling secret file outside it, registers the handler exactly as documented, and requests the sibling file through encoded `..` path segments.

```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "os"
    "strings"

    "github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/web"
)

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{AppDir: os.Args[1], Dev: false}))
    for _, target := range []string{
        "http://example/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/secret.txt",
        "http://example/secret.txt",
    } {
        rr := httptest.NewRecorder()
        req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", target, nil)
        mux.ServeHTTP(rr, req)
        fmt.Printf("%s => status=%d location=%q contains_secret=%v body=%q\n",
            target,
            rr.Code,
            rr.Header().Get("Location"),
            strings.Contains(rr.Body.String(), "ancestor-secret-marker"),
            rr.Body.String(),
        )
    }
}
```

Maintainer-runnable clean-checkout recipe:

```sh
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$tmp/root/a/b/app"
printf 'ancestor-secret-marker' >

items.summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.
items.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation

items.summary: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.
items.title: When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary

items.summary: Security tools raise findings across cloud environments, and AI agents now investigate and prioritize them. A finding is still resolved by people: it has to reach the people responsible for fixing it and accountable for the resource it concerns. Ownership is the organizational context that decides who that is. Where recorded, it is declared by hand in configuration management databases or owner tags and goes stale unless kept current; accounts are shared, and automation creates much of the infrastructure. The knowledge sits in work records, code history, audit logs and identity directories, encoded in each organization's own conventions. Recovering it poses four challenges: the signal is scattered across sources, none of them authoritative; the conventions that carry it differ between organizations; reaching an owner takes multi-hop links; and those related to a resource differ in the strength of their relation. We define ownership as a set of entities, people or teams, each related to the resource by one of five patterns ordered by strength. We present a reference architecture for agentic ownership attribution that derives ownership from these records instead of declaring it: it profiles an organization offline into tested signal procedures and an ownership playbook, then attributes each resource with a coordinator agent and parallel investigators, with confidence computed by rules. On 100 resources of 50 Amazon Web Services (AWS) resource types in one organization, we pool the architecture's candidates with those of an unprimed general-purpose agent and verify every evidence piece against the records. The architecture reaches 92.1% weighted recall and 86.6% weighted precision, against 54.8% and 77.4%, at 0.55 times the agent's cost per unit of coverage. The difference lies in people who build and change resources without an explicit owner, found through work records and code history.
items.title: Agentic Attribution of Cloud Resource Ownership

items.summary: As post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards evolve, developers must adapt implementations, tests, and protocols. Studying this work requires connecting code changes to problem reports and developer reviews. We present PQC-Corpus, a dataset of linked development histories from 179 public GitHub repositories, spanning cryptographic libraries and general-purpose projects. It connects issues and closing pull requests to commits and full patches, with comments and reviews. We combine Git histories with GitHub threads, reconstruct 23 pull-request commit lists truncated at 250 entries, and check file integrity, schemas, and links. Two annotators independently assessed sampled commits and issues ($κ=0.86$ and $0.93$), labeling about seven in ten commits and two in three issues PQC-related within these samples. We provide full and filtered views with removal ledgers, and quantify how filtering reduces links from issues to commits. A patch-free view supports inspection before downloading patches, while traversal scripts follow issues to code changes. We make the dataset and collector publicly available for studies of specification changes, hybrid interoperability, cryptographic review, and migration assistance.

First, we provide an overview of 25 confirmed cyberattacks against universities in German-speaking areas between February 2022 and February 2023. A notable technique is that the phishing emails are sent via university infrastructure, using valid, compromised credentials of university-associated personnel and involving university Virtual Private Network (VPN) tunnels.

items.summary: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer. We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering. The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.
items.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design

items.summary: It is often desirable to generate and release synthetic graphs, which resemble real-world data, in a privacy-preserving way. While substantial progress has been made in designing private graph synthesizers (PGS), opportunities remain for more explicit connections between synthesizer models and privacy evaluation, and better accounting for output variation. This paper proposes GSynPEF, a practical framework for empirical evaluation of privacy and utility in settings for which a real-world graph is given as input and output synthetic graph(s) are observed. Our framework links a broad class of graph synthesizers (both statistical and deep-learning based) with privacy metrics, expanding evaluation dimensions to practical utility and risk, through empirical analysis of multiple actual outputs. The framework accommodates both an Exact Solution scenario, where synthesizer behavior is directly observable, and a Monte Carlo Approximation scenario where only synthetic outputs from a black box synthesizer are available. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets and seven widely used graph synthesizers demonstrate framework's versatility, enabling privacy evaluation for different attack goals (e.g., to infer an edge or node) and capabilities (e.g., observing one or multiple synthetic graphs). We analyze evaluation results by examining the relationship between graph statistics and synthesizer design choices, providing insights for data curators in PGS selection and researchers for improved PGS design.
items.title: GSynPEF: A Privacy Evaluation Framework for Synthetic Graphs

items.summary: Broken Access Control (BAC) has been the foremost category in the OWASP Top Ten since 2021, primarily due to the challenges in enforcing authorization at the application layer. Traditional mechanisms depend on logic embedded in the application, referencing relational database information such as permissions, roles, or ownership. However, missing or incorrect checks can go undetected by external systems, leaving applications vulnerable. This paper presents BACGUARD, a reverse proxy designed to enforce authorization for unmodified applications. BACGUARD reconstructs authorization relations by leveraging authenticated user data from session stores and object ownership from relational schemas. It evaluates whether users are permitted to access resources and blocks unauthorized requests in real time. Unlike existing approaches, BACGUARD bases its authorization on database joins, making the system resilient to forgery. For most requests, decisions are made deterministically. In cases where access control violations are only apparent in response data, such as cross-user data leakage, a language model is used as a fallback. Evaluations on six applications, including those with known vulnerabilities, demonstrate that BACGUARD's hybrid deterministic and language model-based approach blocks all tested attacks with a false-positive rate below 0.7%. Competing solutions like Web Application Firewalls are less effective and more disruptive. The results highlight BACGUARD's primary contribution: the external reconstruction of authorization facts, enabling robust enforcement even when the application itself is flawed.
items.title: BACGUARD: Fact-Grounded Runtime Mitigation of Broken Access Control

items.summary: Commutative operads have been proposed as a platform for public-key cryptography, with protocols for key agreement, key exchange, encryption and authentication, together with a masking technique and families of algebras with secret parameters intended to strengthen them. We show that breaking key agreement, key exchange and encryption reduces to two problems over the centralizer of the public operations: an interpolation problem for key agreement and a division problem for the other two. Neither problem requires recovering a secret, and the set from which secrets are drawn plays no role in these attacks. For the operad platforms in the two original papers (fields, the integers, residue rings, the tropical semiring with finite entries, convexors and the masked tropical algebras), the relevant problems can be solved in polynomial time in the input models specified here, and masking does not affect these attacks. The authentication protocol fails for a more elementary reason: as originally stated it does not bind the prover to any public key, and even with a registered public key the response expected by the verifier can be computed from public data. In the masked variant, verification requires the secret mask; on the concrete string platforms, one observed session with an invertible challenge entry suffices for forgery. We also observe that one of the auxiliary constructions satisfies the algebra axioms only in a degenerate case, although the corresponding protocol remains correct. The attacks are implemented and verified on random instances of representative platforms.
items.title: Cryptanalysis of operad-based cryptography

items.summary: Deep learning training is difficult to verify within a scientific workflow: its architecture, hyperparameters, and procedure are rarely fixed until training has been attempted, and two honest runs never produce the same weights, so recomputation cannot serve as a check. We present SciCheck, a framework in which the scientist explores training configurations freely and posts a blueprint to a provenance ledger for each candidate they want verified, and a verifying scientist judges the resulting run in two layers: a statistical judge model that compares per-step gradient statistics against the verifier's own reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly chosen training segments whose checkpoints are committed to the ledger one epoch at a time. On an MLP, a CNN, and an autoencoder at 100k-500k parameters, under gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fabricated runs, SciCheck reaches F1 of 0.966, 0.906, and 0.976 while rejecting 0-4.4% of honest runs. For the attacks we test, the spot-check accounts for most of this accuracy, and we characterize what each layer can detect. The effective-signal statistic falls as $(1-2s)^2$ under a sign flip of severity $s$, so gradient statistics alone catch strong enough sign flips, while fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics look no more anomalous than honest runs to any statistical detector we test. The spot-check catches fully fabricated segments with probability at least $1-(1-s)^k$ for $k$ sampled segments when the draws stay hidden until the run is committed, which roughly matches our measurements and lets a verifier choose $k$ for a target soundness. Verification costs 1.5-2.3x one retraining, mostly for the verifier's reference run; each submission's spot-check takes under 1.5 s, and per-epoch commitments reduce checkpoint storage 5-17x compared with keeping every checkpoint.
items.title: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training

items.summary: Concept erasure, or concept unlearning, in text-to-image diffusion models is usually audited with prompt attacks. A prompt attack tests whether one conditioning string still retrieves the erased concept. It does not measure the probability that the frozen generator still assigns to that concept. We introduce least-action auditing of this residual probability, and evaluate it on Stable Diffusion concept-erasure checkpoints. The least-action barrier is the minimum control cost of driving the frozen reverse process into a detector-defined concept event. This cost equals the path-space KL divergence of conditioning the model on the event, and therefore the event's negative log-probability. The estimate $ΔS_{\mathrm{rob}}$ uses a CLIP$\wedge$DINOv2 consensus terminal, with no retraining and no adversarial prompt. Across $18$ erased concept-mechanism pairs spanning object classes and NSFW nudity, $ΔS_{\mathrm{rob}}$ predicts deployment leakage counted on $1{,}500$ fresh samples per model by detectors excluded from the audit (pooled Spearman $ρ{=}{-}0.76$, $p{=}5{\times}10^{-4}$). Within every audited concept, the eraser with the higher barrier leaks less ($18/18$). On NSFW nudity the barrier orders the standard erasers exactly: UCE $ΔS_{\mathrm{rob}}{=}3.9$ (leak $16.4\%$) $<$ ESD $75.5$ ($9.8\%$) $<$ RECE $224.5$ ($1.4\%$), while Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) stays near zero and leaks $85.5\%$ under explicit prompts. The same trajectories repair deployed checkpoints. An audit-guided closed-form patch reduces UCE nudity leakage from $16.2\%$ to $0/1{,}500$ and RECE church leakage by $3.3\times$, where direction-count-matched random edits fail.
items.title: Beyond Prompt Attacks: Least-Action Auditing of Concept Erasure

items.summary: We study a safety harness that improves itself without touching model weights. Enmo Safety wraps a chat model with a deterministic input assessment, trigger-matched safety guidance, spotlighting of untrusted content, and an output guard. A reflector model turns failures into one bounded update per round, and an update is kept only if it lowers harm without raising refusal of benign prompts on a held-out dev split. Every version is snapshotted and every decision ledgered. We evaluate a bare model, the seed harness and the evolved harness on six open benchmarks (HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, AgentHarm, deepset prompt-injections). On 150 items and on a 290-item holdout, none of the before/after differences on two models was statistically significant. A fourth iteration ran six policy models on a fresh 300-item split: the harness cut the unsafe rate significantly on two models (12.9% to 7.1%, p = 0.035; 10.2% to 3.6%, p = 0.036), not on the other four, and raised agentic-harm labels on two. Whether the rules fired was unrelated to outcome (Fisher p from 0.30 to 1.0), and the helpfulness clauses made agentic harm worse than no harness on obfuscated attacks. A reworded clause and an input-normalisation step form harness v22, at a measured cost in benign tool-task refusal. Each cell is one run, so these estimates do not establish a general safety improvement. Code, harness versions and ledger: https://github.com/rioryugen/enmo_safety

items.summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) connects information across documents through entity relationships to support relational reasoning. However, black-box access to GraphRAG systems can enable adversaries to reconstruct knowledge graphs and recover both structural connectivity between entities and the semantics of their relationships. Existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees and provide limited protection against such reconstruction attacks. We propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, which provides formal privacy guarantees by mitigating connectivity leakage and protecting relations and their semantic meaning through relation removal. We formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds the distinguishability of mechanism outputs according to the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal. Building on this definition, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitizes source documents before GraphRAG indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing their associated connectivity using the exponential mechanism. Experiments across three GraphRAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks demonstrate that RelGuard provides stronger protection against reconstruction attacks than four existing defense mechanisms while better preserving downstream utility.
items.title: Differentially Private GraphRAG: Protecting Relation Connectivity and Semantics

items.summary: Zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to prove the correctness of a statement or execution of a computation while revealing no more than the statement of correctness itself. Recent use cases, such as AI datasets, suggest the need for faster proof generation over increasingly large constraint sets. This paper explores efforts in optimizing zero-knowledge proof generation, specifically PlonK, using GPUs, for applications that are not amenable to solution via incrementally verifiable computing (IVC). Our intention with this work is to improve ZK performance by introducing fundamental changes in the low-level architectural structure of proof generation. These changes affect performance curves for most current proof generation algorithms. In particular, this paper explores the trade-offs between increased parallelization on GPUs and the resultant memory management problems that occur due to this parallelization. We implement a parallelized PlonK in order to analyze these trade-offs and make arguments concerning the nature of data flows within the proving protocol. Our results lead us to consider multi-GPU environments to maximize performance for large circuit sizes. Such environments introduce issues of communication, efficient hardware management, data partition, and data transfers. This paper further discusses the use cases that motivate multi-GPU implementations, their cost models, and the use of remote direct memory access (RDMA) for data transfer among GPUs.
items.title: Performance Bottlenecks in Computing ZK Proofs on a GPU

items.summary: Explanation APIs are often treated as increasing model-extraction risk, but an end-to-end attack comparison cannot show whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or merely supplies a convenient next-query coordinate. We study this distinction for explanation-guided extraction of tabular classifiers. We separate an explanation into an attribution channel, which ranks influential features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values for perturbing those features. We then test whether the useful bin edges are privileged to the service or reproducible from the adversary's own data. Across six datasets and five target families, using attribution rankings to choose which features to perturb provides no systematic extraction advantage. Lime's discretization bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 percentage points on continuous features, but those edges are quantiles of the explainer's background data rather than properties of the target model. In controlled comparisons, an attacker-side grid reproduces the useful bin-edge gains without querying an explanation API. We use these findings to derive Cutpurse, which combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 percentage points on continuous-feature targets. It also exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 percentage points. Thus, withholding default Lime bin edges alone does not prevent effective extraction under the in-domain auxiliary-input, probability-output, and same-family surrogate assumptions studied here. Our results concern default Lime and Shap configurations for tabular classifiers. They do not establish the same conclusion for other explainers, target classes, or data-free attackers.
items.title: Cutpurse: Decomposing Explanation-Guided Model Extraction on Tabular Data

items.summary: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) models increasingly require data, more publicly available yet licensed data is being harvested and used without authorization. Although several previous studies have proposed watermarking methods for dataset copyright auditing, their applicability to the text-to-image (T2I) setting remains notably limited. The core drawback is that watermarks embedded by existing techniques are often treated as noise and are gradually filtered out and attenuated during the latent noising-denoising process of diffusion model training. We propose NotaryMark, to our knowledge the first multi-bit watermarking method specifically designed for black-box auditing of T2I training dataset use. The core idea of NotaryMark is to align the watermark with the latent denoising of diffusion models, thereby overcoming the signal decay that plagues existing multi-bit methods during sampling. We evaluate NotaryMark across three datasets and three diffusion models spanning watermark capacities from 8 to 1024 bits. With a watermark capacity below 32 bits, it achieves a high average bit accuracy of 0.85-0.90. With a watermark capacity exceeding 32 bits, it maintains bit accuracy between 0.67 and 0.80, consistently outperforming existing multi-bit watermark methods whose bit accuracy is around 0.42-0.60. Furthermore, we design a voting-based aggregation scheme to boost the bit accuracy with a modest budget of 30 queries. Building on this, we incorporate error-correcting codes to enable reliable decoding and tracing of the embedded identifier information. Robustness evaluation against fifteen evasion attacks spanning seven categories shows that NotaryMark remains robust under most evaluated settings, while stronger attacks generally suppress watermark evidence only at the cost of substantial utility degradation, demonstrating its practical reliability against malicious tampering.
items.title: NotaryMark: Multi-Bit Watermarking for Black-Box DatasetUsage Auditing in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

items.summary: Pocket ID is an OIDC provider that allows users to authenticate with their passkeys to services. From 2.2.0 until 2.12.0, SendEmailVerification uses the token model in backend/internal/model/email_verification_token.go to bind an email-verification token only to the user's identifier, while UpdateUser can change the account email without invalidating the outstanding token and VerifyEmail marks the current address as verified. An ordinary user can request a token for an address they control, change the account to an arbitrary unused address, and redeem the old token so Pocket ID publishes the new address with email_verified set to true. The default affected configuration uses emailsVerified=false and allowOwnAccountEdit=true; the target address must not already belong to another Pocket ID user. A relying application that trusts a verified email for automatic account matching or provisioning can link the attacker's identity to another user's account, while applications that rely exclusively on the stable OIDC sub claim are not affected by that downstream consequence. This issue is fixed in version 2.12.0.

items.summary: FreeSWITCH is a Software Defined Telecom Stack enabling the digital transformation from proprietary telecom switches to a software implementation that runs on any commodity hardware. Prior to 1.11.3, sofia_presence_handle_sip_i_message() split the To user of an inbound SIP MESSAGE on a plus sign and treated the left side as a chat protocol selector. Selecting the api chat proto reached switch_api_execute(), allowing a peer whose MESSAGE was accepted to run FreeSWITCH API commands, including operating-system command sinks, with the daemon's privileges. Inbound chat is enabled on the stock internal and external profiles, and any authenticated profile account is sufficient; stock directory users without password material can also remove that barrier in affected configurations. The flaw permits configuration and credential disclosure, arbitrary call control, and command execution, and exploitation has been observed in the wild. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.3.

items.summary:
Issue summary: Calling the OpenSSL API function SSL_free_buffers may cause
memory to be accessed that was previously freed in some situations

Impact summary: A use after free can have a range of potential consequences such
as the corruption of valid data, crashes or execution of arbitrary code.
However, only applications that directly call the SSL_free_buffers function are
affected by this issue. Applications that do not call this function are not
vulnerable. Our investigations indicate that this function is rarely used by
applications.

The SSL_free_buffers function is used to free the internal OpenSSL buffer used
when processing an incoming record from the network. The call is only expected
to succeed if the buffer is not currently in use. However, two scenarios have
been identified where the buffer is freed even when still in use.

The first scenario occurs where a record header has been received from the
network and processed by OpenSSL, but the full record body has not yet arrived.
In this case calling SSL_free_buffers will succeed even though a record has only
been partially processed and the buffer is still in use.

The second scenario occurs where a full record containing application data has
been received and processed by OpenSSL but the application has only read part of
this data. Again a call to SSL_free_buffers will succeed even though the buffer
is still in use.

While these scenarios could occur accidentally during normal operation a
malicious attacker could attempt to engineer a stituation where this occurs.
We are not aware of this issue being actively exploited.

The FIPS modules in 3.3, 3.2, 3.1 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue.

items.summary:
In server mode pgAdmin 4 locks an internal account after MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS failed logins (3 by default). The limit could be bypassed, giving an unauthenticated attacker an unlimited number of password guesses against any internal account, including the administrator's, in the default configuration:

- Flask-Security registers its own views next to pgAdmin's. A login submitted to its /login view was checked and logged in without pgAdmin's failed login count or lock. Its /verify view checked a signed-in user's password without limit, its /change view changed a password without pgAdmin's change password permission or re-encrypting the user's saved server passwords, and its /reset views sent and applied password resets for accounts that are not internal or are locked.
- The internal account was looked up by its exact username, while the login form matches the email ignoring case, so a login with the username typed in another case was neither counted nor checked for the lock.
- With LDAP or webserver authentication also configured, a wrong internal password was never counted, and with Kerberos or webserver authentication configured a guess could be answered without being counted.

In addition, where accounts from different authentication sources share an email address, a password reset could be sent for, or applied to, an account from another source, and the About box showed the server configuration to a user whose email was that of an administrator's account.

The fix refuses submissions to Flask-Security's own views, counts every failed internal login however the username is typed and whatever other sources are configured, no longer lets a login that posts a password fall back to an authentication source that does not check it, and locks only internal authentication. Password resets and the About box act only on the user's own internal account. Desktop mode is not affected.

This issue affects pgAdmin 4: before 9.19.

items.summary:
In server mode pgAdmin 4 resolves a server's password file, SSL certificate, key, CRL and SSH tunnel identity file relative to the user's storage directory, but get_complete_file_path() only stripped leading slashes before joining the two. A path such as "../<another user>/.pgpass", set through the server dialog, the REST API or a servers.json import, therefore named another user's file, and connecting used that user's saved passwords, client certificate or SSH key. The sslkeylogfile connection parameter was passed to libpq unchanged, so a path outside storage let libpq create or append a file as the account running pgAdmin.

make_conninfo() also quoted connection parameter values but not their names, so a crafted parameter name could smuggle additional keyword=value pairs past these checks.

The fix requires the resolved path, with symbolic links followed, to stay inside the user's storage directory or the named shared storage directory, confines sslkeylogfile the same way, and accepts only exact libpq keywords as connection parameter names. A refused path or keyword is reported instead of letting libpq fall back to a default.

This issue affects pgAdmin 4: before 9.19.
